When to repot, and when not to

The safest time for most houseplants is early spring to early summer, when the plant is about to grow and can recover quickly. Avoid repotting a plant that is stressed, newly bought, or in the middle of flowering unless the roots have clearly run out of room; give new plants a few weeks to settle first.

Go up only one size — roughly one to two inches (2–5 cm) wider than the current pot. A much larger pot holds a volume of wet soil the roots cannot use, and that soil stays wet long enough to rot them. If a plant is top-heavy but the roots are fine, a heavier pot of the same size solves the problem without the risk.

  • Water the day before; moist roots slide out and tolerate handling better.
  • Loosen circling roots with your fingers; cut away any that are brown, mushy, or smell sour.
  • Keep the plant at the same soil depth it was before, and hold off on fertilizer for a month or two.

Signs it is time to repot

SignWhat it usually meansRepot?
Roots growing out of the drainage holes or circling the surfaceRoot-boundYes, up one size
Water runs straight through and the plant dries out within a day or twoRoots have replaced most of the soilYes, up one size
Plant tips over easily; pot lifts with the root ball in one pieceRoot-bound and top-heavyYes, up one size or a heavier pot
Soil is compacted, crusty, or smells sourOld mix has broken downYes — same size pot, fresh mix
Slow growth in spring with healthy leavesCould be light or feeding, not rootsCheck roots first
Plant looks fine, pot looks smallMany plants prefer being slightly snugNot yet

Soil mix by plant group

What to write in the Soil mix column, and what to buy. Proportions are by volume and approximate.

Plant groupMix that worksWhy
Tropical foliage (pothos, dracaena, peace lily)Potting mix with about one part perlite to three parts mixHolds moisture but drains
Aroids (monstera, philodendron, alocasia)Chunky: roughly equal parts potting mix, orchid bark, and perliteAir around thick roots; dries evenly
Succulents & cactiCactus mix, or potting mix cut 50/50 with grit or pumiceDries fast; no wet feet
Orchids (phalaenopsis)Orchid bark, sometimes with a little charcoal or sphagnumRoots need air and light
Ferns & calatheaPeat- or coco-based mix with a little perliteStays lightly moist
African violetLight violet mix or peat with perlite and vermiculiteFine roots, needs to stay airy

How to use this sheet

  1. Print the PDF and file it with your plant records, or keep it with the potting supplies.
  2. Each time you repot, write the date, the plant, and the old and new pot diameters — measured across the top.
  3. Note the mix you used (even 'store cactus mix + perlite') so you can repeat what worked or fix what did not.
  4. Describe the roots in a few words: white and firm, circling, brown and mushy, sparse. This is the diagnostic value of the sheet.
  5. Set Next check one to two years out, or sooner for fast growers, and look at the sheet each spring.

Questions

Is this sheet really free?

Yes. The PDF is free to download and print — no sign-up, no email, no watermark.

How often do houseplants need repotting?

Most every one to two years; slow growers and succulents every two to three. Let the signs in the table decide rather than the calendar — some plants flower better slightly root-bound.

Can I reuse old potting soil?

For the same plant in a larger pot, mixing some old soil with fresh is fine if it is not compacted or sour. Replace it entirely if the plant had root rot or pests.

Why did my plant droop after repotting?

Transplant shock is normal for a week or two, especially if roots were trimmed. Keep it out of direct sun, water lightly, and do not fertilize until new growth appears.
